headline: Britain sends jets to Saudi Arabia. Defensive, it says.
summary: Britain said Tuesday it will send fighter jets to protect Saudi cities, airports and energy sites from Houthi missiles and drones fired out of Yemen. London calls the patrols defensive, and an expansion of help it already gives. The Houthi strikes have turned deadly, and on Monday Saudi Arabia postponed its flagship investment conference.

cover_question.q: Are the planes going to fight?

cover_answer: Britain says no. They guard the sky, they don't attack.
table_question: If a friend is being hit, is standing guard the same as fighting?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: Some planes from Britain are flying to Saudi Arabia, a country an ocean and most of a day's flight away, to help keep its cities safe from flying machines sent to hurt them. The pilots' job is to watch the sky, the way a crossing guard watches the road. The grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A crossing guard is a guard they already know. The rest stays an ocean away.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid feature for the whole event, here the flying machines, so the script gives them the crossing guard to look at instead and puts the rest an ocean away. Shielded, because this is a war and a child this age reads your face before your words. Expect "could one come here?" No. The patrols are over Saudi Arabia.

8-12.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
8-12.script: The Houthis, an armed group in Yemen backed by Iran, have fired drones and missiles at Saudi airports and oil sites, and people have died. Saudi Arabia put off a big investment conference. Then Britain said it would send jets to patrol the sky. A goalkeeper: there to block shots, not take them.
8-12.why: Strikes, a put-off conference, jets. A goalkeeper ends the chain.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out cause and effect, so the script hands them a chain: the strikes, the postponed conference, the jets. The goalkeeper is the mechanism, and it carries the word "defensive" without a lecture. Expect "why does Britain care?" AP says Britain is expanding support it already gives. None of the articles say why.

13-17.script: Britain calls the patrols defensive. Does the word still hold once British pilots are in the fight? The Houthi strikes have hit Saudi airports and energy sites and killed people, and the kingdom just postponed its showcase investment conference. When does guarding a country's sky become fighting its war?
13-17.why: Defensive is a word doing a job. Let them test it.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the jets are there to stop attacks, and sending them puts British pilots in a war. The script asks them to test the word "defensive" rather than accept or mock it, the argument skill Kuhn says improves with practice. Expect "so is Britain at war now?" The articles don't say. Neither should you.

5-7.q: Are the planes going to fight?
5-7.a: Britain says no. They fly over Saudi cities to keep drones and missiles away. It's far from here.

8-12.a: An armed group in Yemen that Iran backs. They've fired drones and missiles at Saudi Arabia.

8-12.q: Why did Saudi Arabia cancel its conference?
8-12.a: It postponed it as the strikes got worse. The articles say no more.

13-17.a: Britain says the patrols are defensive. The articles stop at that word.

13-17.q: Why is Saudi Arabia being attacked?
13-17.a: The Houthis are hitting airports and energy sites, symbols of the kingdom's ambitions, Semafor says.
